3.1: Arjuna's confusion: if knowledge is superior, why do you push me into this terrible action?
3.2: Your words seem contradictory and bewilder me — tell me the one path by which I may attain the highest.
3.3: Krishna names two paths in this world: knowledge for the contemplative, action for the active.
3.4: Not by abstaining from action does one attain freedom, nor by renunciation alone does one reach perfection.
3.5: No one can remain even for a moment without acting; nature's qualities compel everyone to act.
3.6: One who sits restraining the organs while the mind dwells on objects is a hypocrite, not a yogi.
3.7: But one who controls the senses with the mind and engages in action without attachment excels.
3.8: Do your allotted work; action is better than inaction — you could not even maintain your body without it.
3.9: The world is bound by action except when it is done as sacrifice; do your work in that spirit, free from attachment.
3.10: Having created humanity along with sacrifice, the Creator said: by this shall you prosper and gain your desires.
3.11: Nourish the gods with sacrifice and they will nourish you; by mutual nourishing you attain the highest good.
3.12: Fed by sacrifice, the gods give you desired enjoyments; one who enjoys without giving back is a thief.
3.13: The good who eat what remains after sacrifice are freed from sin; those who cook only for themselves eat sin.
3.14: The chain of dependence: beings from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice, sacrifice from action.
3.15: Action arises from the Veda, the Veda from the Imperishable — so the all-pervading is ever centred in sacrifice.
3.16: One who does not follow this turning wheel lives in vain, delighting in the senses.
3.17: But one who delights only in the Self, satisfied and content in it, has no duty to perform.
3.18: Such a one has nothing to gain by doing or not doing, and depends on no being for anything.
3.19: Therefore always perform your duty without attachment — acting without attachment, one attains the Supreme.
3.20: Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone; act also for the guidance of the world.
3.21: Whatever a great person does, others follow; the standard they set, the world pursues.
3.22: Krishna's own example: there is nothing in the three worlds I need to gain, yet I act.
3.23: If I did not act tirelessly, people everywhere would follow my example.
3.24: If I stopped acting, these worlds would perish; I would be the author of confusion and destroy all beings.
3.25: As the ignorant act with attachment, so the wise should act — but without attachment, for the good of the world.
3.26: Do not unsettle the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action; act well yourself and inspire them.
3.27: All actions are performed by nature's qualities; deluded by ego, one thinks 'I am the doer'.
3.28: The knower of truth sees that the senses merely move among sense objects, and is not attached.
3.29: Those deluded by the gunas cling to their works; the wise should not unsettle these dull-witted people.
3.30: Surrender all actions to Me, free of longing and selfishness, and fight without mental fever.
3.31: Those who follow this teaching with faith and without cavil are freed from the bondage of action.
3.32: Those who carp at it and do not practise it are deluded, senseless and doomed.
3.33: Even the wise act according to their own nature; beings follow their nature — what will restraint accomplish?
3.34: Attraction and aversion sit in each sense; do not fall under their power — they are the enemies on the path.
3.35: Better one's own duty though imperfect than another's well performed; death in one's own duty is better.
3.36: Arjuna's sharp question: what compels a person to commit sin, even against their own will, as if by force?
3.37: Krishna names the enemy: desire, and the anger born of rajas — all-devouring and all-sinful.
3.38: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust, an embryo by the womb, so is knowledge covered by this.
3.39: Knowledge is covered by this constant enemy of the wise — desire, an insatiable fire.
3.40: The senses, mind and intellect are its seat; through them it deludes the embodied by veiling knowledge.
3.41: Therefore first control the senses and kill this sinful destroyer of knowledge and realisation.
3.42: The ladder of subtlety: the senses are superior to the body, mind to the senses, intellect to the mind — and the Self is above the intellect.
3.43: Knowing the Self as beyond the intellect, steady the self by the Self and slay this hard-to-conquer enemy of desire.
